name: Plyometrics

lead: Plyometrics is training built on quick, forceful movements such as jumps and bounds that use the stretch-shortening cycle: a muscle lengthens then shortens rapidly. Soviet researcher Yuri Verkhoshansky developed the original shock method in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

People add it to training to build explosive power and an athletic build. Research includes meta-analyses comparing it with weightlifting and resistance training, and trials on neuromuscular programs that include jumps and injury rates in athletes.

paras: Typical sessions use box jumps, bounds and landings, and are placed alongside strength work. Athletes in basketball, volleyball and sprinting use them regularly.

The forces are high, so Wikipedia advises that plyometrics be done by well-conditioned people, ideally supervised. Depth jumps from platforms above about 75 cm are described as often counterproductive and injury-prone.

angle.text: Plyometrics train explosive power and landing control, and people add them to strength programmes when they want the muscular, athletic look and movement of jumpers and sprinters. They are one component of a physique plan alongside lifting, conditioning and nutrition.

lead: Plyometrics, often shortened to plyos, is a style of training built on maximum-intensity explosive movements, mostly jumps and bounds but also throws, slams and clap push-ups, in which a muscle is rapidly stretched and then rapidly shortened [1]. The mechanism is the stretch-shortening cycle: the landing stretches muscle and tendon and stores elastic energy, and a very fast switch into the takeoff returns it as force, with much of the stretching and recoil occurring in the tendons [1].

For appearance, people use plyometrics as part of training for an athletic, powerful, lean lower body and a sporty build, alongside lifting and conditioning. The chain is training-based: jumps and bounds load the legs and trunk quickly, power and jumping ability rise, and the trainee carries the look and movement quality of a jumper or sprinter. It is a mainstay in sprinting, jumping events, basketball, volleyball, football codes and martial arts [1].

The method was developed in the Soviet Union, where Yuri Verkhoshansky created the depth-jump based shock method in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and was named in the United States in the early 1980s by former Olympic runner Fred Wilt [1]. Research includes meta-analyses comparing it with weightlifting and resistance training [2], trials of injury-prevention programmes that include jumping [3][4], and reviews of its use in volleyball [5] and sports physical therapy [6].

paras: Plyometric exercises are performed at maximal intensity with minimal contact time, so that the muscle lengthens and shortens in rapid succession [1]. Lower-body examples include squat jumps, tuck jumps, box jumps, lateral jumps, single-leg hops, bounding, broad jumps and depth jumps. Upper-body examples include plyometric push-ups, medicine-ball chest passes and overhead slams, and full-body options include jump rope and power skipping [1].

Variants are grouped as maximal (such as depth jumps), serial (repeated jumps in one direction), lateral, rotational, combination, rhythmic, loaded (with vests or barbells) and unilateral, the last being used to check for strength imbalances between legs [1]. The term has become broad: sources note it is often used as a buzzword for nearly any jump, and that simple jumping used as a warm-up is generally not true plyometric work because ground contact is too slow [1].

The stretch-shortening cycle has three phases. In the eccentric phase, the athlete lands and the muscles lengthen under load, storing energy. In the amortization phase, the brief transition from landing to takeoff, the stored energy is redirected; it is generally described as needing to be about 0.20 seconds or less, with world-class sprinters near 0.08 seconds. In the concentric phase the muscles shorten to produce the upward drive, with hip, knee and ankle extension contributing in sequence [1]. A slow transition lets the stored energy dissipate as heat, which is why contact time is emphasised [1].

A 2025 review of how tissues respond to loading notes that recovery time differs between tissues, and that tendons which have undergone high stretch-shorten cycle activity benefit from a refractory period of around 48 hours [7].

Soviet Olympians used plyometric-style training from the 1950s [1]. Yuri Verkhoshansky developed the shock method in the late 1960s and early 1970s, with the depth jump, dropping from a raised platform and immediately jumping upward, as its central exercise; his 1966 and 1967 articles in Legkaya Atletika describe the work [1]. Fred Wilt, a former US Olympic distance runner, coined the term plyometrics in the early 1980s after watching Soviet athletes jump during warm-ups, and teamed with Michael Yessis, who had worked with Verkhoshansky, to spread the method in the United States [1].

Books helped codify it: Radcliffe and Farentinos published Plyometrics: Explosive Power Training in 1985 and Donald Chu published Jumping into Plyometrics in 1998 [1]. A 1997 letter in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy, titled Pondering plyometrics, discussed the concept in the physical therapy literature [8]. Wikipedia notes that the original shock method has largely been forgotten in the US as the word came to cover most jumping [1].

Plyometrics are used by sprinters, high jumpers, martial artists and players of basketball, tennis, badminton, squash, volleyball and football codes, and to a lesser extent in general fitness [1]. Lifters combine them with weightlifting and heavy resistance work, which a 2022 meta-analysis of 16 studies and 427 participants compared for strength, power and speed [2].

Trainers commonly describe explosive work as the complement to maximal strength: heavy lifting builds force capacity and jumps train the speed at which it is applied. A T Nation forum post on power training, for example, lists leaps, bounds, jumps and slams as plyometric options next to dynamic lifts such as snatches and cleans.[9]

Low-intensity plyometrics are used in injury rehabilitation [1], and a review of return to play after posterior cruciate ligament injury says that return-to-play algorithms include plyometrics and sport-specific training [10]. A 2020 randomized trial, ACL-SPORTS, examined a secondary injury-prevention programme in female athletes [4].

A 2022 systematic review with meta-analysis in Sports Medicine compared weightlifting training with traditional resistance training and plyometric training on strength, power and speed, pooling 16 studies of 427 participants and converting results to Hedges' g effect sizes [2]. A 2019 systematic review covered 21 intervention studies of plyometric training in volleyball players, in which vertical jump was the most commonly studied outcome and young female athletes the most studied group [5].

A 2022 randomized trial in female college athletes examined combining plyometric and balance exercises for dynamic balance [11], and a 2019 randomized trial in elite youth footballers compared one versus two weekly plyometric sessions for jump, sprint and change-of-direction ability [12]. A 2023 cluster randomized trial found that a multicomponent neuromuscular warm-up reduced lower-extremity injuries in trained basketball players [3]. Wikipedia also cites a 12-month randomized trial by Hinton and colleagues (2015) in which high-intensity jump training increased bone mineral density at the lumbar spine and whole body in men with low bone mass, and a study by Ebben and colleagues (2011) that compared muscle activation, power and force across ten plyometric exercises, finding single-leg cone hops, box jumps, tuck jumps and two-legged vertical jumps produced among the highest muscle activation [1]. A 2015 concepts article reviews plyometric exercise for sports physical therapy [6].

Human studies cover athletes' jump, sprint and agility performance [5][12], balance [11], injury-prevention programmes that include jumping [3][4], bone density in men with low bone mass [1] and comparisons against weightlifting and resistance training [2]. Study populations are mostly athletes and trained participants, with volleyball players, basketball players, footballers and college athletes the commonly studied groups [3][5][12][11].

Plyometrics produce large forces and are described as appropriate for well-conditioned people, ideally with supervision, adequate strength, flexibility and proprioception, and technique taught before progressing [1]. Chu (1998) recommended a baseline of 50 squats at 60 percent of body weight before starting [1]. Prepubescent and older participants are described as needing special consideration [1].

For depth jumps, Wikipedia describes beginners starting around 30 cm and progressing to 50 and 75 cm, notes Verkhoshansky considered 100 cm the maximum for high-level athletes, and states that heights above 75 cm are usually counterproductive and risk injury. Excessive depth jumping is described as causing fatigue and, according to Verkhoshansky, sleep disturbance [1].

Plyometrics appear in fitness communities as part of athletic-physique and vertical-jump training, typically within broader lifting and conditioning routines [1]. Forum material on the topic is mostly general strength-and-power discussion rather than a dedicated looksmaxxing doctrine.
